\chapter*{The Bengali script --- a reference}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{The Bengali script (reference)}
\markboth{Bengali script}{Bengali script}

A \textbf{reference}, not a chapter — the lessons teach reading through real words. This page gathers the system and flags what is special about the \textbf{Bengali script} and Bengali sounds.

\section*{How the Bengali script works (the three facts)}

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
\setlength{\itemsep}{0.35em}
  \item \textbf{Consonants carry a built-in vowel — and it is ô, not \textquotedblleft{}a\textquotedblright{}.} \bn{ক} = kô, \bn{ন} = nô, \bn{ম} = mô — written left to right under a connecting top line, like Devanagari but with rounder shapes. This single fact (\emph{a$\to$ô}) is why Sanskrit words sound \textquotedblleft{}Bengali.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{A vowel sign changes it:} \bn{কা} kā · \bn{কি} ki · \bn{কী} kī · \bn{কু} ku · \bn{কে} ke · \bn{কো} ko. The \emph{i}-signs \bn{ি} / \bn{ী} are written \emph{before} the consonant but read \emph{after} it. A \emph{chandrabindu} \bn{ঁ} nasalises the vowel.
  \item \textbf{Standalone vowels have their own letters:} \bn{আ} ā · \bn{অ} ô · \bn{ই} i · \bn{উ} u · \bn{এ} e · \bn{ও} o — used when a word starts with a vowel.
\end{enumerate}

\section*{What is special about Bengali sounds}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
\setlength{\itemsep}{0.35em}
  \item \emph{\textbf{s\emph{ $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}sh\textquotedblright{}.\textbf{ \bn{স} (and \bn{শ}, \bn{ষ}) is usually pronounced \textquotedblleft{}sh\textquotedblright{}: \bn{আসি} is \emph{āshi}, not \emph{āsi}.}}}}
  \item \textbf{No separate \emph{v} or \emph{w}.} Bengali has only \bn{ব} \emph{b}, so Sanskrit \emph{vāda} $\to$ \emph{bād}, \emph{Vishnu} $\to$ \emph{Bishnu}. This \emph{v$\to$b} shift is a Bengali signature.
  \item \textbf{Conjuncts.} A \emph{hasanta} (\bn{্}) strips a consonant's vowel so it fuses with the next: \bn{স্} + \bn{ক} $\to$ \bn{স্ক}, \bn{চ্} + \bn{ছ} $\to$ \bn{চ্ছ}. Many conjuncts take special shapes learned as you meet them.
\end{itemize}

\section*{Bengali in the family}

Bengali (\emph{Bāṅlā}) is \textbf{Indo-Aryan} — from Sanskrit, like Hindi, Marathi, and Punjabi — and its script descends, with Devanagari, from the old Brahmi writing of India, which is why they share the hanging top line. Spoken across West Bengal (India) and Bangladesh by some 250 million people, it carries an immense literary tradition — Tagore's poetry, and the national anthems of \emph{two} countries, the only tongue that can say so. The lessons trace its Sanskrit roots and, where they reach, the wider Indo-European family that also shaped English.
